newsitem.title: GERMANY: Graf's father must stay in detention - court.
newsitem.headline: Graf's father must stay in detention - court.

text.p: A German court ruled on Tuesday that Peter Graf, father of tennis star Steffi Graf, must stay in jail while he is tried for tax evasion.
In a ruling read out at the trial in Mannheim, the high court in Karlsruhe said there was still a danger that Peter Graf, 58, and family tax adviser Joachim Eckardt might try to flee the country.
"To lift the detention order would seriously endanger the trial," the ruling said.
This overturned the decision of the Mannheim court, which had ordered Graf freed on bail of three million marks ($2 million), and Eckardt on bail of 300,000 marks.
"There is no basis for this decision," said Graf's lawyer Peter Salditt. "The higher court only looked at documents and did not form a personal impression of my client."
Peter Graf has been in detention since August last year and went on trial in Mannheim earlier this month.
He is accused, together with family tax adviser Joachim Eckardt, of evading 19 million marks of taxes on his multimillionaire daughter's earnings between 1989 and 1993.
Graf, who was known for collecting his daughter's fees in cash in plastic bags, admits diverting 42 million marks abroad out of the reach of German tax collectors.
But he says the authorities signalled their approval of his tax schemes on the basis that this would prevent Steffi joining an exodus of German sporting tax exiles.
The world number one player herself remains under investigation, although she says she left her financial affairs to her father from an early age.
She says prosecutors are waiting for the outcome of her father's trial to decide whether to drop the investigation against her in return for payment of a fine.

Peter Graf faces a maximum sentence of 10 years, but legal experts say the fact that the Mannheim court was ready to free him on bail suggests he is not expected to be jailed for more than five years if convicted.
State prosecutors had appealed against the Mannheim court's ruling, arguing that Graf might try to flee the country, and he stayed in prison while the higher court made its decision.
